title: Multidisciplinary care models for managing pregnancies complicated with chronic diseases: A systematic review
content:
by Gayani Shashikala Amarasinghe, Sucharitha Rangi Weerasuriya, Christina Malatzky, Sanjeewa Kularatna, William Parsonage

Multidisciplinary care is a key recommendation for the management of complicated pregnancies in contemporary obstetrics, but how to implement it in the real world remains unclear and poorly supported by research evidence. This systematic review describes the characteristics and outcomes of multidisciplinary care models for managing pregnancies complicated with chronic diseases. PubMed/Medline, Embase, and CINAHL databases were searched for relevant studies published between January 2013 and January 2026. Studies were included if they described a multidisciplinary care model in which multiple clinical disciplines interacted during pregnancy. Reporting quality was assessed with the TIDieR checklist. The risk of bias and the certainty of evidence were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tools and the GRADE tool. Of 8515 screened articles, 51 were included. Characteristics and outcomes were synthesized narratively. Models varied widely in team composition, communication patterns, and decision-making processes. Specific characteristics, including model design, performance monitoring, and funding, were described inconsistently. Available evidence on effectiveness was limited. There was very low-certainty evidence that multidisciplinary care reduced maternal mortality in women with chronic disease. Reduced maternal and fetal morbidity was also reported. Clinicians and policymakers can use this collective description to select strategies for effective multidisciplinary care models appropriate for the socio-economic, health system, and disease-related context of their specific setting. Studies with robust methodology would provide stronger evidence supporting multidisciplinary care during pregnancy. Standardized reporting of multidisciplinary care provision is also important for deriving sound conclusions about the effectiveness of the models and their adaptability across different health systems.
